w .From '-BeWs Weekly Messenger London, November 28, 1812. Every hour is pouring in further particulars, official and private, of our late victories in China and Affghanistan. We pass over the account given in the dispatch of the military position and strength ot Nankin, a city 20 miles in circumference the only two particulars of any importance are, that it is a city nearly as large and populous þÿas London, containing one million of inhabitants, and surrounded and girded in by a wall varying from 70 to 28 feet :n height, having four principal gates, the approach to which was along so many broad causeways, or roads raised above the marshes and rice grounds amidst which the city is situated. In the middle of the city is an inner town or citadel occupied solely by the Tartars, it being the policy of the Chinese government, which is the reigning Tartar dynasty, to keep the Tartars and Chinese as separate as possible, and to trust entirely to its Tartar subjects for the defence of the empire. þÿ Here, thereþÿfore, says General Gough, þÿ l was fully a ware that the in tin stand would be made in the Tartar city ; 1 understood also, that the Tartar garrison amounted to about six thousand men, all trained to arms, and perhaps the most formidable opponents, as they would hive to tight for their families and their homes," The total of the British force, a portion being Indian sepoys, amounted þÿ four thousand five hundred men. to only But l saw," continued General Gough, þÿ that 1 should have no difficulty in breaking open cne of the gates, and thus forcing mv way into

the Chinese town. I saw also a height within the walls, which commanded the citadel or Tartar town, and J therefore felt no doubt, that ur >n effecting mv entry into the Chinese city, an ! thence carrying m v cannon up to the top of this hill, i should immediately compel the surrendet of the Tartar town and citadel, or take it by þÿassault. Though the advance of the armament reached Nankin, as above said, on the morning of the 4h of August, the whole force v;ns not assembled in front of the city until the 1 0 th. O.i the three following days the soldiers and marines were landed, and were placed in positions on one or other of the four roads which led to the gates of the city 'These prepai ations were continued downtothe l'ih. lb the coume ot mat dav flu; general received a letter from Sir H. Bollinger, requiring him to suspend hostilities, as three imperial coni missionets Had arrived with sufficient powet'3 to conclude a peace.

The government of India directed its army to pass the Indus in order to expel from Afghanistan n chief believed to be hostile to British interests, and to replace upon bis throne a sovereign represented to be fiiendly to those interests, and popular with his former subjects. The chief believed to be hostile became a prisoner, and the sovereign represented to be popular was replaced upon his throne; hut, after events which brought into question his fidelity to the government bv which lie was restored, he lost by the hands of an assassin the throne he had only held amidst insurrections and his death was preceded and followed by still existing anarchy. Disasters unparalleled in their extent, unless By the errors in Which they originated, and by the treachery by which they were completed, have in one short campaign been avenged upon every scene of past misfortune ; and repeated victories in the field, and the captiire of the cities and citadels of Ghuznee and Catml, have again attached the opinion of invincibility to the British arms. The I! itish artnv in possession of Afghani- «1an will now be withdrawn to the Sutlej.

To force a sovereign upon a reluctant people would he as inconsistent with the policy as it is with the principles of the British --government, tending to place the aims and resources of that people at the disposal of the first invader, and to impose the burden of supporting a Sovereign without the prospect of benefit from his alliance The Governor General will willingly recognise any government approved by the Affghans themselves, which shall appear desirous and capable of maintaining friendly relations with neighbouring states. Content with the limits nature appears to have assigned to its empire, the government of India will devote ad its effects to ihe establishment and maintenance ol general peace, to the protection of the sovereigns and chiefs its ailies, and to Lite prosperity and happiness of its own faithful subjects The rivers of the Puujaub and the Indus, and the mountainous passes and ihe barbarous trifies of Afghanistan, wi I oe placed between the British army and an enemy approaching the west, if indeed such an enemy there ran be, and no longer between the army and its supplies. The enormous expendi ure required for the support of a large tmee. in a false military position, at a distance Irom its own frontier and its resources, will no longer arrest every measure for the improvement ol the country and of the people.

The combined army of England and of India, superior in < quipinent. discipline, valour, and in the officers oy whom it is cumii.unded, to any force winch can lie opposed to a in Asia, will stand m ui- assailable atrengih upon its own soil, arid for ever, under the bl ssn g of þÿ1 iOvhience, preserve the glorious empire it has won. in security and in honour. The outbreak of an insurrection in Catalonia, or, to speak more correctly weh reference to the late disturbances, in Barcelona, is an incident which has unhappily been of Inr too frequent occurrence to occasion much suiprise. Nor has this Catalan spirit of revolt been more conspicuous amidst the modern vicissitudes of lite S 1 '«! f I n monarchy i < than in the days of its irux-t absolute pov. or.

Of the fourteen or fifteen sieges which the city of Barcelona has at vaiious times sustained, by far the greater number have been occasioned by the rebellious resistance ol the population to the Generals of the Royal armies ; and the severity of the language which Espartero or his Ministers are reported to have used is readily accounted for, if it be nut wholly justified, by their knowledge of the incorrigible temper of the people arrayed in aims against the Queen's Government. As a political movement, it is impossible to conceive a more ill regulated and incomprehensible demonstration of a desire to do mischief. without either a scheme or a ieader to give effect to the brutal passions of an ignorant multitude. But the combustible elements which are so well known to exist iri the city and the province doubtless attracted the machinations of those foreign incendiaries, whose cause is irrecoverably lost if, in spite of their predictions and conspiracies, Spain remains tranquil, and the Government of this Regent uuassailed by weapons more formidable than those of constitutional debate.

Jn the arts of life, and particularly in those of carpentry, in smttheiv and in masonry, mining, and the breaking and training of domestic cattle; if we assume that these arts have about seven stages from their commencement to their European perfection, the Chinese in each of these arts have advanced about three stages Thus in mining thev know how to dig up the metal, and vei y rudely to clear it of clav, and to convert ir into solid one. þÿ But they have no machinei y to clear the mines of any irruption of w ater, and therefore tliev abandon them at once when any such accident takes place. In their cattle also, their fl <cks and their herds, they are In low every other civilised nation in the world; their horses are always useless in war, and the staple of their food are the veriest vermin of the þÿearth cats, dogs, serpents, and every speed s of carrion. In carpentry, they have if le axe. the saw, and (fie plane; but they execute with the knile what in Europe is done with the chisel, and they have none of those tools by which the European woiktren executes bis grooviugs, (lutings, fittings, and other finished workman-ship, la smithci y. also, they know the use of the forge,

the anvil, the bellows, pincers tor holding the metal, and hammers for working it. But all the more delicate workmanship, such as is done at Birmingham by machinery, they work up laboriously by their hands ; imitating, o as they can, the models which thev " have got from other countries, and thus wasting as much labour on the production of a ring or a screw as in Europe would produce 10.0(10 of them in the same time. In masonry, also, they know nothing of assisting the manual powers by the aid of machinery ; nothing of the pulley : nothing in short of the art of raising immense masses by machinery ; accordingly everything is dime by the manual labour of multitudinous hands. Thus, through their great public works are built of masonry, liecause their despotic government, like the ancient Egyptian monarcs, can here make a levy of the people en masse to accomplish then; almost all their private hotfesure built of wood, an. I their only decorations are painting , varnishes, and carvings, by the knife þÿ Their furniture is, also, m the same taste; mere benches, forms, and carved bedsteads and couches, la manufactures, or to use a more proper word, clothing, they are equally behind all other European nations in respect to the use of machinery ; they know nothing of cotton & silk mills, spinning jennies, &c In Europe our manufacturing process has been long distributed into the five branches, spinning (inclusive of carding), weaving, fulling, dyeing, and as regards hides and skins, dress-
ing and tanning, and all of these amongst us arc executed by distinct bodies of workmen' each applying himself singlv to bis own parti-

cular process, such as spinners, weavers, fullers, dyers, and tanners. In China, no such division of labour is known, and fn m their ignorance of machinery, all spinning and weaving is done by single hands and single looms. In two other minor arts, indeed, connected with these, that of embroidery, or w orking by the needle, figures in re lief upon a plain ground, with coloured threads, or gold or silver tissue, and also in carpet work, or that of weaving with coloured yarns, in the same piece, they very greatly excel, but still by means of the same laborious labour. In china and pottery, also, they have attained a great excellence, arid in the art of founding, they imitate European models with great perfection. Such, if we except their stereotype printing, is the summary of lire auvance they have made in art. þÿ

þÿ þÿ þÿ From the St. Thomas Times, Feb. 22, 1843. On Monday last H. B. M ship Illustrious, 74 guns bearing the Hag of Vice-Admiral Sir Charles Adam, commanded by Captain Erskine in company with the brig of war Pilot 16 guns Commander Houston, arrived at this port from Antigua, and exchanged salutes with Fort Christian. þÿ In the course oi the morning, the gallant Admiral landed at the þÿKing wharf s where he was received by a guard of honor, and greeted with a salute of 15 guns. During the commencement of the week we bad the curiosity to pay the Marine Repairing Slip a visit, so far as our knowledge extends in mechanical pursuits we could not but admire this high spirited undertaking, we say high spirited, because it is the most extensive work our island ran boast of. and we believe emanates more from a patriotic Seeling ol our Merchants and Inhabitants than the immedi ate motive of gain, winch such an establishment could produce þÿ that the work has cost considerably more than the first average, can in no means create surprise to any individual, who like ourselves may pay the Slip a visit, for on simple conversation even with one of the labouring people, difficulties (grown out since the commencement) will be shown, which cannot fail to satisfy them that unforeseen as they unavoidably must have been when the plans were first formed, offer sufficient and reasonable apology for the supporters and builder of this undet taking, for ail the delay and exira costs. The second dam, (the first being long since completed and the rails laid down) is now in

operation, and has for a time baffled all the skill and perseverance which could be applied, and proved itself the most stubborn portion of the work, but time the cure,' of al' evils has performed its duly and we begin to see favourable prospects of a speedy completion to the undertaking þÿ as little or nothing remains to be done after the darn is completed We cannot conclude our remarks without expressing our satisfaction to the Directors for their continued exertions, as well as to Mr. Thomas Matthew, engineer and builder, to whom all praise is due as a skilful experienced mechanic both in theory and in practice.

If the tears of Africa have elicited the sympathy and called forth the successful efforts ol those who profess to be the friends of the suffering and the succour of the oppressed, surely we may have expected those sympathies to have been awaksued, and that succour to have been extended to these people, whose land has been taken from them, and who are in a stale ol moral degradation disgusting to leflect on. The late trial of four of them for the murder of one oi their own tribe, afforded a striking illustration of the total absence of ttiose principles of natmal theology which arc to be found in m my savage nations, as well as of the exisience among them of gross piejudices and barbarous superstitions. We have never conversed with any person, who, however otherwise well acquainted with them, could give us any information of their apprehension of the being of a God. The extent of their religion seems to he the belief of a future state, to which ail must eventually go, and of the power ol Obeah. Their ideas of a future

state are, simply þÿ that there is a world beyond this, in which ell men must at last assemble, but that the passage to it is lengthened according to the amount of our evil needs in this ; they say that the good go at once to it, but the bad, in proportion to the extent of the evil they have committed, have a tedious and painful journey thither. Their laith in the power of Obeah and the Evil Eye is great indeed. Matthias, the interpreter, was ..sked by a gentleman why they went behind Jan to shcot him, and he replied, that they did so to prevent being killed by meeting the look ol his eye3. They also believed that by his incantations fie had introduced the small pox among them. All þÿ England, Ireland, Scotland, YVale( and Berwick upon 'i þÿweed, are in a state ol gieat fomentation and excitement, in consequence of the tidings received by the Inst oriental mail, of the perfect triumph of ihe British arms in China and Affghauistan. The idea that China would ever enter into a bond of þÿ peace and þÿfriendship with any nation of those þÿ baiharians," whose linle island (to wit, England, France and America,) not almost imperceptibly the vast ocean that encircles the celestial Empire, on its own maps, would have been a ween ago deemed a

prc|Osterous impossibility. That the might, by superior military science, and a fearful I atteiy from the engines of civilised warfare, be compelled to acknowledge the existence oi other rights and interests than their own, was certainly consideied among things remotely possible; bu> that ibey should consent to treat on a þÿ footing of perfect þÿepuality wilh any other power, and subscribe to conditions mutually advantageous, and involving an unlimited import and export trade, was not conceivable. The effects of these conquests on ihe political condition of Great Britain are literally vast. The present ministry inherited from their predecessors two wars, one of which they condemned as impolitic, while they denounced both as iniquitous. þÿ Neither wa . however, in a state to permit abandonment, without serious derogation from the dignity of the British crown, and a consequent weakening of its moral power in the Cast. The intelligence of the past week fim therefore relieved the government from the necessity of prosecuting two distant wars of great expense of doubtful issue, and ol wore than doubtful expediency and justice. It in thought that Sir Robert Feel will be able, o.i the strength oi the Chinese tribute, and þÿ hi cessation of the wars which rendered or. unpopular impost necessary, to discontinue before long his sorely abused þÿ income þÿlax.; thus removing one great cause of dislike to the present administration among thenucdling classes of society ; while, on the other hand,

it is anticipated that a market will be opened in China for Biitish fabrics, which wii! speed ilv relieve the distress of the operatives, and quiet the revolutionary feeling of the manufacturing districts. Auspicious as are the events just rrsada known to us. doubtless the advantages likely to accrue therefrom are somewhat over estimated, in the first flush oi a great and unexpected triumph. As respects the relief to the icver.ue, and the consequent ability to remove the income ta:;. it must be remembered that though the expense of actively prosecuting these wars has ceased, the very expensive process of retracing the hostile steps taken, and of withdrawing and r-eiransporting troops, lias yet to firs performed þÿ an achievement second onlv in cost and diffieultv to tiie outfit and despatch oi a hostile armament for the commencement of a campaign. Besides, the Chinese indemnification is to he paid by instalments during three years, and a very considerable British force is to be maintained in that countiy until all the money is paid and ail \he stipulations of the treaty are fulfilled. Thus it appears that the expenses of the war :...ve by no mean? ceased, and that the twenty one millions of money from the Chinese, being div.nLute d over a space of more than three years, will give no very sensible aid to the revenue. in regaid to the market likely to he opened for Bniish muiiUiaaiuics in China, I confess myself any thing but sanguine. The population of China is so fearfully

dense and labour is so proportionality r.hosip, that no English production can contend with those of China for genet ai consumption A single piece of tie cheapest kind ol British goods, at its minimum price, would form a respectable dowry for a Chinese female, and lie <qunl in value to enough of a Chinese labile ui ordinary use, to clothe a smafl army

of Celestials. Independently, however, of the fact that competition with their domestic fabrics in point of price is rendered almost impracticable by the cheapness of labour among the people, it is a well known and indisputable fact, that no people in the world are so impervious to any thing like novelty or so prejudiced against every thing foreign, as these worthy gentlemen in pig-tails. Even Spanish dollars, (to the importation of which it must be confessed they make no violent opposition,) are deprived as soon as may be of their foreign uniform and chopped up into unintelligible bits of bullion, adopted to Chinese taste, and looking for all the world like so many peripatetic letters of their never-to bethoroughly comprehended alphabet. There appears to be no stipulation in the treaty relative to the establishment of permanent diplomatic intercourse between the two countries. Singular Accident. Past Monday two gentlemen took a horse from the stable of Air. Sewaid, known as þÿ Rob þÿHoy, and drove, out to Woburn. On their return the horse became unmanageable, ran, and escaped from his drivers, tie returned to Woburn. Search was made for him, hut he was no where to he fomnl þÿ On Thursday, after a search of three days, lie was found lying in a ravine, about half a mile from Horn pond, in the midst of briars and stones, completely exhausted. The sleigh w as still attached to him. He lived but a few minutes alter he was discovered. He must have died of starvation and cold.

A Newfoundland dog accompanied one of the gentlemen on the eventful Monday evening. When the sleigh was overturned and the horse ran awnv, the dog pursued him, and was by when he fell into the briars. During the whole of Tuesday the dog employed himself in going backward and tor ward between the horse and a farm house in the neighborhood within a stone's throw, endeavoring to attract the attention of the inmates of the latter. An Earthquake unexampled in vour annals, spread has ruin and desolation over our unhappy land every where buildings destroyed, every where victims of this tremendous disaster are visible. The city of Point a Pet re no longer exists ! Innumerable d -ad bodies lie buried under its ruins, from which you have extricated more than fifteen hundred wounded, miraculously saved. Your calamity is great, but every resource is not destroyed, all hope is not lost. Already your brothers of Martinique, and their worthy Governor, have extended the friendly hand, already the brave Admiral, with whose svmpaihies you have becnsolong and to partake "t vour labors He divides acquainted, has a. rived, to share þÿ in your grit! with you the provisions of Iris fleet. France will hear your cries, and your calamities and distresses will lorce her tears, goon, the benefactions of the Throne, do not doubt it. will arrive to solace your suflerings; goon, the mother country will fly to the aid of her childien, now without bread, and without shelter. Pot a nearer resource has been preserved to you bv Providence. It is the Props, yet on the ground, and which must be saved. Among the wrecks ot fallen works, von will find the necessary materials to rebuild xnanv. þÿ Combineyour efforts ; employ them to repair the Mills which have the least suf-

fered and to restore those buildings, which by their position, may serve several Estates. And soon, your produce embarked in the Ships which await them, will give you the means of passing less painfully those long months, which must elapse, before the national generosity will arrive to succour us. It is thus, you will lighten the weight of misery from your families, which you have faced without fear, and have suppoited with a noble resignation. The administration is engaged in providing lor tbe principal wants of the present; but prudence requires that we should regard the future ; that tfie inhabitants of the country should free I v plant ground provisions, and thus renew the limited stock which they have so generously shared. With their unhappy brethren of Point ii Petrc. Inhabitants of Guadeloupe ! I admire vour Courage and your resignation under nuslnrtune. In your persevering efiorts to eflace all traces of inis disaster, ifie noble children of France will he recognized. Over the ruins of Point a Petre, February 1 1 ih 1843. II. Those who hold the doctrine that the federal Government is bound to provide a currency; and that this was one of Hie chief objects which the constitution was made to eflect. Those who contend that a department of the government can be established, if there be an earnest desire to do so, which can furnish the tequired currency, without resorting to a national bank, lo this class the i icsidem, Mr. Webster, Mr. Tallmadge, Mr Cushing, Mr. Saltonstall, Mr. Winthrop and otliers belong. PEEL. þÿ The right hon. baronet proceeded, " You ask us what we have done for lite purpose of relieving the distresses oi the country ? We have done other things, or at least attempted to do other things, than the mere reduction of the Customs' duties We have besn in office about lo months, and 1 think we have a right to look back upon what has been effected during that period w ithout any sense of shame (cheers). We have succeeded in terminating two wars (cries of Oil !" responded to by " cheers on the ministerial side of the house). V\ hether it may have been owing to the wisdom of our measures or not, the noble lord (Palmerton) wiil not at least deny that we have had the good fortune to bring to a successful termination two wars, which were necessarily absorbing the capital of this country in unproductive labour, which were, as ail wars most do, striking a double blow, by diverting our own resources and consuming the re sou: ces o! those countries with which we ate to canyon a commercial intercourse. \\ c hope to effect a reduction >n the estimates of the present year (hoar. hear). \\ e trust that we shall bo enabled in the present session to present estimates on the turec great branches of naval, military, and civil service, which will show a reduction of about 850,000/. We have at least, then, begun the process of reducing the estimates. For the last three or four years there has been, perhaps, necessarily and unavoidably, a constantly pro-

gressive increase of expenditure and diminution in the revenue of the country. In the present session we shall commence what, I hope, will be a continued series of diminished estimates (cheer). V\e have been enabled to reduce the military force in (lanada bout 4000 men. and we trust that peace has been established ir. that colony. We are delighted wiili the prospect of establishing a perfect amity wiin France. We have diminished the duties upon colonial produce in every case where it entered into competition with our own, and we have thus made some ad- Vance towards the system of treating our colonies as integral parts of the empire (hear) We have labored to effect, and 1 trust successfully, an adjustment of those differences with the United States which had continued for 40 years, which have only been exasperated hv delays, and which were the main causes for apprehending the disturbances oi our peaceful relations wiih that country. We tried to settle those differences without any compromise of British honour, and, on the other hand, without exciting such a feeling of hostility towards this country as appears to exist in some portions ol the trench nation.
